speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on achieving our dual-mandate goals of maximum employment and stable prices for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our economy is strong overall and has made significant progress toward our goals over the past two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market has cooled from its formerly overheated state.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased substantially from a peak of 7 percent to an estimated 2.2 percent as of August.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re committed to maintaining our economy’s strength by supporting maximum employment and returning inflation to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the Federal Open Market Committee decided to reduce the degree of policy restraint by lowering our policy interest rate by ½ percentage point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This decision reflects our growing confidence that with an appropriate recalibration of our policy stance, strength in the labor market can be maintained in a context of moderate growth and inflation moving sustainably down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also decided to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has continued to expand at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP rose at an annual rate of 2.2 percent in the first half of the year, and available data point to a roughly similar pace of growth this quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Growth of consumer spending has remained resilient, and investment in equipment and intangibles has picked up from its anemic pace last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the housing sector, investment fell back in the second quarter after rising strongly in the first.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Improving supply conditions have supported resilient demand and the strong performance of the U.S. economy over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, Committee participants generally expect GDP growth to remain solid, with a median projection of 2 percent over the next few years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the labor market, conditions have continued to cool.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Payroll job gains averaged 116,000 per month over the past three months, a notable step-down from the pace seen earlier in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate has moved up but remains low at 4.2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has eased over the past year, and the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Overall, a broad set of indicators suggests that conditions in the labor market are now less tight than just before the pandemic in 2019.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is not a source of elevated inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection for the unemployment rate in the SEP is 4.4 percent at the end of this year, four-tenths higher than projected in June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased notably over the past two years but remains above our longer-run goal of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.2 percent over the 12 months ending in August and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.7 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecasters as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation is 2.3 percent this year and 2.1 percent next year, somewhat lower than projected in June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thereafter, the median projection is 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our monetary policy actions are guided by our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For much of the past three years, inflation ran well above our 2 percent goal, and labor market conditions were extremely tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our primary focus had been on bringing down inflation, and appropriately so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are acutely aware that high inflation imposes significant hardship, as it erodes purchasing power, especially for those least able to meet the higher costs of essentials like food, housing, and transportation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our restrictive monetary policy has helped restore the balance between aggregate supply and demand, easing inflationary pressures and ensuring that inflation expectations remain well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our patient approach over the past year has paid dividends: Inflation is now much closer to our objective, and we have gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As inflation has declined and the labor market has cooled, the upside risks to inflation have diminished, and the downside risks to employment have increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We now see the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals as roughly in balance, and we are attentive to the risks to both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In light of the progress on inflation and the balance of risks, at today’s meeting, the Committee decided to lower the target range for the federal funds rate by ½ percentage point to 4¾ percent to 5 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This recalibration of our policy stance will help maintain the strength of the economy and the labor market and will continue to enable further progress on inflation as we begin the process of moving toward a more neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are not on any preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy restraint too quickly could hinder progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing restraint too slowly could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering additional adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path for the federal funds rate, based on what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy evolves as expected, the median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 4.4 percent at the end of this year and 3.4 percent at the end of 2025.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These median projections are lower than in June, consistent with the projections for lower inflation and higher unemployment, as well as the changed balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These projections, however, are not a Committee plan or decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As the economy evolves, monetary policy will adjust in order to best promote our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy remains solid and inflation persists, we can dial back policy restraint more slowly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the labor market were to weaken unexpectedly or inflation were to fall more quickly than anticipated, we are prepared to respond.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Policy is well positioned to deal with the risks and uncertainties that we face in pursuing both sides of our dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed has been assigned two goals for monetary policy—maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to supporting maximum employment, bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal, and keeping longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our success in delivering on these goals matters to all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to your questions.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Steve.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Steve Liesman, CNBC.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for taking our questions.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: In July, you said you weren’t necessarily thinking about a 50.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: You didn’t want to be specific, but you said you weren’t thinking about a 50.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: The inflation data last week came out a little firmer than expected.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Retail was strong, third-quarter GDP running 3 percent.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: So what changed that made the Committee go 50, and how do you respond to the concerns that perhaps it shows the Fed is more concerned about the labor market?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And I guess, should we expect more 50s in the months ahead?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: And based on what should we make that call?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, okay, a lot of questions in there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Laughter] Let me jump in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, since the last meeting—okay, the last meeting we have had a lot of data come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve had the two employment reports, July and August.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve also had two inflation reports, including one that came in during blackout.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had the QCEW report, which suggests that maybe—that not maybe, but suggests that the payroll report numbers that we’re getting may be artificially high and will be revised down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve also seen anecdotal data, like [the data collected in] the Beige Book.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we took all of those, and we went into blackout.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we thought about what to do, and we concluded that this was the right thing for the economy, for the people that we serve, and that’s, that’s how we made our decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s one question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What was the second and third?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: How do we make the—sorry, thank you, sir.

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: How do we figure out in the months ahead, is there another 25 or 50 coming in based on what should we make that call?

speaker: STEVE LIESMAN
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A good place to start is the—is the SEP, but let me start with what I said, which was that we’re going to be making decisions meeting by meeting based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at the SEP, you’ll, you’ll see that it’s, it’s a process of recalibrating our policy stance away from where we had it a year ago, when inflation was high and unemployment low, to a place that’s more appropriate given where we are now and where we expect to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that process will take place over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s nothing in the—in the SEP that suggests the Committee is in a rush to get this done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This, this process evolves over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, that’s a projection.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a baseline projection.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know, as I mentioned in my remarks, that the actual things that we do will depend on the way the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can go quicker if that’s appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can go slower if that’s appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can pause if that’s appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s, that’s what we are contemplating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, I would point you to the SEP as just an assessment of where—what the Committee is thinking today—what the individual members, rather, of the Committee are thinking today, assuming that their particular forecasts take—you know, are realized.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Let’s go to Chris.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Hi.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Chris Rugaber at Associated Press.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: The projections show that the Fed—Fed officials expect the fed funds rate to still be above their estimate of long-run neutral by the end of next year.

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: So does that suggest that you see rates as restrictive for that entire period?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Does that threaten the weakening of the job market that you said you’d like to avoid?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Or does it suggest that maybe people see the short-run neutral as a little bit higher?

speaker: CHRIS RUGABER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it would—the way I would really characterize it is this: I think people write down their estimate, individuals do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think every single person on the Committee, if you asked them, what’s your level of certainty around that, they would say there’s a wide range where that could fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are model-based approaches and empirically based approaches that estimate what the neutral rate will be at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, realistically, we know it by its works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that leaves us in a place where we’ll be—where we expect, in the base case, to be continuing to remove restriction, and we’ll be looking at the way the economy reacts to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’ll be guiding us in our thinking about the question that we’re asking at every meeting, which is, is our policy stance the appropriate one?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know—if you go back, we know that the policy stance we adopted in July of 2023 came at a time when unemployment was 3½ percent and inflation was 4.2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, unemployment is up to 4.2 percent; inflation’s down to a few tenths above 2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we know that it is time to recalibrate our policy to something that is more appropriate given the progress on inflation and on employment moving to a more sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the balance of risks are now even.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is the beginning of that process I mentioned, the direction of which is toward a sense of neutral, and we’ll move as fast or as slow as we think is appropriate in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What you have is our individual—accumulation of individual estimates of what that will be in the base case.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Howard.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Howard Schneider with Reuters.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: How close was this in terms of the decision?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: You do have the first dissent by a Governor since 2005, I think.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Was the weight clearly in favor of a 50, or was this a very close decision?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we had a good—a good discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, if you go back, I talked about this at Jackson Hole, but I didn’t address the question of the size of the cut and left it open, and I think we left it open going into blackout.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so there was a lot of discussion back and forth, good diversity of—excellent discussion today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think there was also broad support for the decision that the Committee voted on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would add, though, look at the SEP. All 19 of the participants wrote down multiple cuts this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: All 19.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a big change from June, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Seven of the—seven of them wrote down three or more and—sorry, 17 of the 19 wrote down three or more cuts, and 10 of the 19 wrote down four or more cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, there is a dissent, and there’s a range of views, but there’s actually a lot of common ground as well.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Follow-up to that.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Now that this is in the books, can you give us some guidance as sort of a follow-up to Steve on the pacing here?

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Would you expect this to be running every other meeting once we get into next year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to take it meeting by meeting, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s no sense that the Committee feels it’s in a rush to do this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We made a good, strong start to this, and that’s really, frankly, a sign of our confidence—confidence that inflation is, is coming down toward 2 percent on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That gives us the ability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can, you know, make a good, strong start.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—and I’m very pleased that we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To me, the logic of this, both from an economic standpoint and also from a risk-management standpoint, was clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think we’re going to go carefully, meeting by meeting, and make our decisions as we go.

speaker: HOWARD SCHNEIDER
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jeanna.

speaker: JEANNA SMIALEK
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: JEANNA SMIALEK
sentence: Jeanna Smialek, New York Times.

speaker: JEANNA SMIALEK
sentence: Thanks for taking our questions.

speaker: JEANNA SMIALEK
sentence: You and your colleagues in your economic projections today see the unemployment rate climbing to 4.4 percent and staying there.

speaker: JEANNA SMIALEK
sentence: Obviously, historically, when the unemployment rate climbs that much over a relatively short period of time, it doesn’t typically just stop—it continues increasing.

speaker: JEANNA SMIALEK
sentence: And so I wonder if you can walk us through why you see the labor market stabilizing, sort of what’s the mechanism there?

speaker: JEANNA SMIALEK
sentence: And what do you see as the risks?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, again, the labor market is actually in solid condition, and our intention with our policy move today is to keep it there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You can say that about the whole economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The U.S. economy is in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s growing at a solid pace, inflation is coming down, the labor market is in a strong pace, we want to keep it there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s what we’re doing.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Sorry—Nick.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Nick Timiraos of the Wall Street Journal.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Chair Powell, does today’s action constitute a catch-up in action given recent substantial revisions to the employment data, or is this larger-than-typical rate cut a function of the elevated nominal level of the policy rate such that an accelerated cadence could be expected to continue?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay, multiple questions in there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say we don’t think we’re behind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do not think—we think this is timely, but I think you can take this as a sign of our commitment not to get behind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s, it’s a strong move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sorry, your other question was?

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: It was, is this about what happened in the employment data between this meeting and the last meeting?

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: Or is this about the level of the funds rate—the high nominal level of funds rate relative to what might be expected if you’re trying to maintain equilibrium?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think it’s about—we come into this with a policy position that was put in place, as you know, I mentioned, in July of 2023, which was a time of high inflation and very low unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve been very patient about, about reducing the policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve waited.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Other central banks around the world have cut, many of them several times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve waited, and I think that that patience has really paid dividends in the form of our confidence that inflation is moving sustainably under 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that is what enables us to take this, this strong move today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I do not think that anyone should look at this and say, “Oh, this is the new pace.” You know, you have to think about it in terms of the base case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, what happens will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so, in the base case, what you see is—look at the SEP, you see cuts moving along.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The sense of this is we’re recalibrating policy down over time to a more neutral level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re moving at the pace that we think is appropriate given developments in the economy and the base case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy can develop in a way that would cause us to go faster or slower, but that’s what the base case is.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: And, if I could follow up on the balance sheet, in 2019, when you did the mid-cycle adjustment, you ceased the balance sheet runoff.

speaker: NICK TIMIRAOS
sentence: With a larger cut today, is there any—should there be any signal inferred about how the Committee would approach “end state” on the balance sheet policy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, in the current situation, reserves have really been stable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They haven’t come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So reserves are still abundant and expected to remain so for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As you know, the shrinkage in our balance sheet has really come out of the overnight RRP [facility].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think what that tells you is, we’re not thinking about, about stopping runoff because of this at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that these two things can happen side by side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In a sense, they’re both a form of normalization, and so, for a time, you can have the balance sheet shrinking but also be cutting rates.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Colby.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Colby Smith with the Financial Times.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Just following up on Jeanna’s question on rising unemployment.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: Is it your view that this is just a function of a normalizing labor market amid improved supply, or is there anything to suggest that something more concerning perhaps is taking place here, given that other metrics of labor demand have softened too?

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And I guess, in direct follow-up to Jeanna, do you not—why should we not expect a further deterioration in labor market conditions if policy is still restrictive?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think what we’re seeing is, clearly labor market conditions have cooled off by any measure, as I talked about in Jackson Hole, and—but they’re still at a level—the level of those conditions is actually pretty close to what I would call maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re close to mandate, maybe at mandate, on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what’s driving it?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Clearly, clearly payroll job creation has moved down over the last few months, and this bears watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Many—By many other measures, the labor market has returned to or below 2019 levels, which was a very good, strong labor market, but this is more sort of 2018, ’17.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the labor market bears close—bears close watching, and we’ll be giving it that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But ultimately, we think—we believe, with an appropriate recalibration of our policy, that we can continue to see the economy growing, and that will support the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the meantime, if you look at the growth in economic activity data, retail sales data that we just got, second-quarter GDP—all of this indicates an economy that is still growing at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that should also support the labor market over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but again, we’re—it bears watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re watching.

speaker: COLBY SMITH
sentence: And just on the point about starting to see rising layoffs, if that were to happen, wouldn’t the Committee already be too late in terms of avoiding a recession?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re—that’s—you know, our plan, of course, has been to begin to recalibrate and we’re—as you know, we’re not seeing rising claims, we’re not seeing rising layoffs, we’re not seeing that, and we’re not hearing that from companies that that’s something that’s getting ready to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re not waiting for that, because, you know, there is—there is thinking that the time to support the labor market is when—is when it’s strong and not when we begin to see the layoffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s some lore on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the situation we’re in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have, in fact, begun the cutting cycle now, and we’ll be watching—and that’ll be one of the factors that we consider.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, we’re going to look at the totality of the data as we make these decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Michael McKee.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Michael McKee with Bloomberg TV and Radio.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: To follow up on that, what would constitute for you and the Committee a deterioration in the labor market?

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: You’re pricing in, basically by the end of next year, 200 basis points of cuts just to maintain a higher unemployment rate.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: Would you be moving to a more preemptive monetary policy style—rather than, as you did with inflation, waiting until the data gave you a signal?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to be watching all of the data, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if—as I mentioned in my remarks, if the labor market were to slow unexpectedly, then we have the ability to react to that by, by cutting faster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re also going to be looking at our other mandate, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are more—we have greater confidence now that inflation is moving down to 2 percent, but, at the same time, our plan is that we will be at 2 percent, you know, over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and policy, we think, is still restrictive, so that should still be happening.

speaker: MICHAEL MCKEE
sentence: I’m just curious as to how sensitive you’ll be to the labor market, since you forecast we are going to see higher unemployment and it is going to take a significant amount of monetary easing to just maintain it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, what I would say is, we don’t think we need to see further loosening in labor market conditions to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we have a dual mandate, and I think you can take this whole action as—take a step back, what have we been trying to achieve?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re trying to achieve a situation where we restore price stability without the kind of painful increase in unemployment that has come sometimes with disinflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’re trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think you can take today’s action as a sign of our strong commitment to achieve that goal.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Rachel.

speaker: RACHEL SIEGEL
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: RACHEL SIEGEL
sentence: Rachel Siegel from the Washington Post.

speaker: RACHEL SIEGEL
sentence: Thanks for taking our questions.

speaker: RACHEL SIEGEL
sentence: You’re describing this view that you don’t think you’re behind when it comes to the job market.

speaker: RACHEL SIEGEL
sentence: Can you walk us through the specific data points that you found to be most helpful in the discussions at this meeting?

speaker: RACHEL SIEGEL
sentence: You’ve mentioned a couple, but would you be able to walk us through what that dashboard told you, as far as what you know about the job market now?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ll start with unemployment, which is the single most important one probably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re at 4.2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, you know—I know it’s higher than we were used to seeing, numbers in the mid- and even below mid-3s last year, but, if you look back over the sweep of the years, that’s, that’s a low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a very healthy unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And anything in the low 4s is, is a really—is a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Participation is at high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, you know—we’ve had—we’re right—adjusted for demographics for aging, participation’s at pretty high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages are still a bit above what would be their—wage increases, rather, are still just a bit above where they would be over the very longer term to be consistent with 2 percent inflation, but they’re very much coming down to what that sustainable level is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we feel good about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Vacancies over—per unemployed is back to what is still a very strong level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not as high as it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That number reached two to one, two vacancies for every unemployed person.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As measured, it’s now below—it’s around one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s still—that’s still a very good number, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, quits have come back down to normal levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, I could go on and on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are many, many employment indicators.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What do they say?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They say this is still a solid labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The question isn’t the level; the question is that there has been change, particularly over the last few months, and, you know, so what we say is, as the risks, the upside risks, to inflation have really come down, the downside risks to employment have increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and because we have been patient and held our fire on cutting while, while inflation has come down, I think we’re now in a very good position to manage the risks to both of our goals.

speaker: RACHEL SIEGEL
sentence: And what do you expect to learn between now and November that will help inform the scale of the cut at the next meeting?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, more data, the usual.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t look for anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll see another labor report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll see another jobs report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we get a—we might, actually—we get two—we get a second jobs report on the day of the meeting, I think, or no, no, on the Friday before the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and inflation data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll get all this data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll be watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s always a question of, look at the incoming data and ask what are the implications of that data for the evolving outlook and the balance of risks and then go through our process and think, what’s the right thing to do?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Is policy where we want it to be to foster the achievement of our goals over time?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what it is, and that’s what we’ll be doing.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Neil.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Neil Irwin with Axios.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: We’ve only been running a little above 100,000 jobs a month on payroll the last three months.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Do you view that level of job creation as worrying or alarming, or would you be—would you be content if we were to kind of stick at that level?

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: And relatedly, you know, one of the welcome trends of the last couple of years has been labor markets seen coming out through job openings falling, rather than job losses.

speaker: NEIL IRWIN
sentence: Do you think that trend has further to run, or do you see risk that further labor market cooling will have to come through job losses?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, on the job creation, it depends on—it depends on the inflows, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, if you’re having millions of people come into the labor force then, and you’re creating 100,000 jobs, you’re going to see unemployment go up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it really depends on what’s the trend underlying the volatility of people coming into the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We understand there’s been quite an influx across the borders, and that has actually been one of the things that’s, that’s, that’s allowed the unemployment rate to rise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the other thing is just the slower hiring rate, which is something we also watch carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it does depend on what’s happening on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On the Beveridge curve question, yes, so we all felt, on the Committee, not all, but I think everyone on the Committee felt that job openings were so elevated that they could fall a long way before you hit the part of the curve where job openings turned into higher unemployment, job loss.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And yes, I mean, I think we are—it’s hard to know that—you can’t know these things with great precision, but certainly it appears that we’re very close to that point, if not at it, so that further declines in job openings will translate more directly into unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s been—it’s been a great ride down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, we’ve seen a lot of, of tightness come out of the labor market in that form without it resulting in lower employment.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Edward.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Thanks, Chair Powell.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: Edward Lawrence with Fox Business.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: So we’ve heard some speculation that you may be going with the federal funds rate to 3½, maybe under 4 percent.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: There’s basically an entire generation that has experienced zero or near-zero federal funds rate, and some think we’re heading in that direction again.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: What’s the likelihood that cheap money is now the norm?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is a question—and you mean after we get through all of this?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just—great question that we just, we can only speculate about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Intuitively, most—many, many people anyway, would say we’re probably not going back to that era where there were trillions of dollars of sovereign bonds trading at negative rates—long-term bonds trading at negative rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it looked like the neutral rate was—might even be negative, so—and it was—people were issuing debt at negative rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It seems that’s so far away now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My own sense is that we’re not going back to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, honestly, we’re going to find out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, it feels—it feels to me that the neutral rate is probably significantly higher than it was back then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: How high is it?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t—I just don’t think we know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—again, we only know it by its works.

speaker: EDWARD LAWRENCE
sentence: And one more, how do you respond to the criticism that will likely come that a deeper rate cut now, before the election, has some political motivations?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so, you know, this is my fourth presidential election at the Fed, and, you know, it’s always the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re always—we’re always going into this meeting, in particular, and asking, what’s the right thing to do for the people we serve?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we do that, and we make a decision as a group, and then we announce it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s—that’s always what it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s never about anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nothing else is discussed, and I would also point out that the things that we do really affect economic conditions for the most part with a lag.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, nonetheless, this is what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our job is to support the economy on behalf of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, if we get it right, this will benefit the American people significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this really concentrates the mind, and, you know, it’s something we all take very, very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t put up any other filters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think if you start doing that, I don’t know where you stop.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we just don’t do that.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jo Ling.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: I’m Jo Ling Kent with CBS News.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: My first question is, very simply, what message are you trying to send American consumers, the American people, with this unusually large rate cut?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would just say that, you know, the U.S. economy is in a good place, and, and our decision today is designed to keep it there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: More specifically, the economy is growing at a solid pace, inflation is coming down closer to our 2 percent objective over time, and the labor market is still in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So our intention is really to maintain the strength that we currently see in the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ll do that by returning rates from their high level, which has really been—the purpose of which has been to get inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re, we’re going to move those down over time to a more normal level over time.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: Just have a follow-up to that.

speaker: JO LING KENT
sentence: Listening to you talk about inflation moving meaningfully down to 2 percent, is the Federal Reserve effectively declaring a decisive victory over inflation and rising prices?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, we’re not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So inflation, you know—what we say is we want inflation—the goal is to have inflation move down to 2 percent on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, we’re not really—we’re close, but we’re not really at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think we’re going to want to see it be, you know, around 2 percent and close to 2 percent for some time, but we’re certainly not doing—we’re not saying “mission accomplished” or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I have to say, though, we’re encouraged by the progress that we have made.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Catarina.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: Hi.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: Catarina Saraiva with Bloomberg News.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: I just would love to know kind of how the Committee is thinking about the persistence we’ve seen in housing inflation.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: You know, do you think you can return to 2 percent with housing inflation where it is?

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So housing inflation is the—is the one piece that is kind of dragging a bit, if I can say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that market rents are doing what we would want them to do, which is to be moving up at relatively low levels, but they’re not rolling over—the leases that are rolling over are not coming down as much and OER is coming in high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, it’s been slower than we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we now understand that it’s going to take some time for those lower market rents to get into this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, the direction of travel is clear, and as long as market rents remain, you know, relatively low inflation, over time that will show up, just the time it’s taking now, several years rather than just one or two cycles of annual lease renewals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—I think we understand that now, but I don’t think the outcome is in doubt again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As long as market rents remain under control, the outcome is not as in doubt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would say it’s—the rest of the portfolio—or of the elements that go into core PCE inflation have behaved pretty well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, they’re all—they all have some volatility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will get down to 2 percent inflation, I believe, and I believe that, ultimately, we’ll get what we need to get out of the housing services piece, too.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: Some of your colleagues have expressed concern that, with starting to cut rates, you could re-ignite demand in housing and see prices go up even more.

speaker: CATARINA SARAIVA
sentence: What’s the likelihood of that, and how would you react to that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The housing market, it’s hard to—it’s a game that—the housing market is in part frozen because of lock-in with low rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People don’t want to sell their homes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, because they have a very low mortgage, it would be quite expensive to refinance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As rates come down, people will start to move more, and that’s probably beginning to happen already.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But remember, when that happens, you’ve got a seller, but you’ve also got a new buyer in many cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not, you know, obvious how much additional demand that would make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, the real issue with housing is that we have had, and are on track to continue to have, not enough housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so it’s going to be challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s hard to find—to zone lots that are in places where people want to live.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—all of the aspects of housing are more and more difficult, and, you know, where are we going to get the supply?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And this is not something that the Fed can, can really fix.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think, as we normalize rates, you’ll see the housing market normalize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, I mean, ultimately by getting inflation broadly down and getting those rates normalized and getting the housing cycle normalized, that’s the best thing we can do for house holders.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then the supply question will have to be dealt with by the market and also by government.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Victoria.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Hi.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Victoria Guida with Politico.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: Just following up on some of the labor market talk earlier, you know, monetary policy operates with long and variable lags, and I’m wondering how much you see being able to keep the unemployment rate from raising too much comes from the fact that you’re starting to act now and that’s going to give people more room to run versus just the labor market is strong.

speaker: VICTORIA GUIDA
sentence: And then, also, if I could, following up on Nick’s question, do you see today’s 50 basis point move as partially a response to the fact that you didn’t cut in July and that sort of gets you to the same place?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right about lags, but I would just point to the overall economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You have an economy that is growing at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you look at forecasters or talk to companies, they’ll say that they think 2025 should be a good year, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s no sense—the U.S. economy is basically fine if you talk to market participants, I mean, you know, business people who are actually out there doing business.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, you know, I think our move is timely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, as I said, you can—you can see our, our 50 basis point move as a commitment to make sure that we don’t fall behind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re really asking about—your second question, you’re asking about July.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I guess if you ask if we’d gotten the July report before the meeting, would we have cut?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We might well have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We didn’t make that decision, but we might well have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that’s not—you know, that doesn’t really answer the question that we ask ourselves, which is, let’s look, you know—at this meeting we’re looking back to the July employment report, the August employment report, the two CPI reports, one of which came, of course, during blackout, and all of the other things that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking at all of those things, and we’re asking ourselves, what’s the right—what’s the policy stance we need to move to?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We knew—it’s clear that we—clearly, literally, everyone on the Committee agreed that it’s time to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just how big—how fast do you go, and what do you think about the paths forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this decision we made today had broad support on the Committee, and I’ve discussed the path ahead.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Elizabeth.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Elizabeth Schulze with ABC News.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: Mortgage rates have already been dropping in anticipation of this announcement.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: How much more should borrowers expect those rates to drop over the next year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Very hard for me to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s—from our standpoint, I can’t really speak to mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will say that’ll depend on how the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our intention, though, is—we think that our policy was appropriately restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think that it’s time to begin the process of recalibrating it to a level that’s more neutral, rather than restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We expect that process to take some time, as you can see in the projections that we released today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as—if things work out according to that forecast, other rates in the economy will come down as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: However, the rate at which those things happen will really depend on how the economy performs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We can’t see—we can’t look a year ahead and know what the economy is to be doing—going to be doing.

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: What’s your message to households who are frustrated that home prices have still stayed so high as rates have been high?

speaker: ELIZABETH SCHULZE
sentence: What do you say to those households?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, what I can say to the public is that we had the highest—we had a burst of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Many other countries around the world had a similar burst of inflation, and, when that happens, part of the answer is that we raise interest rates in order to cool the economy off in order to reduce inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not something that people experience as pleasant, but, at the end, what you get is low inflation restored, price stability restored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And a good definition of price stability is that people in their daily decisions, they’re not thinking about inflation anymore.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where everyone wants to be, is back to what’s inflation, you know?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Just keep it low, keep it stable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re restoring that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what we’re going through now really restores—it will benefit people over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Price stability benefits everybody over a long period of time, just by virtue of the fact that they don’t have to deal with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what’s been going on, and I think we’ve made real progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I completely—we don’t tell people how to think about the economy, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, people are [still] experiencing high prices, as opposed to high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we understand that’s painful.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Greg.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: Hi, Chair Powell.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: Greg Robb from Marketwatch.com.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: I was wondering if you could go through—you said just at the beginning that, coming into the blackout, there was like an open thought of 25 or 50—you know, the Fed could move either 25 or 50.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: I would sort of argue that when we had those two last speeches by Governor Waller and New York Fed President John Williams, that they were sort of saying that maybe a gradual approach was going to win the day.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: I mean, I sort of want to ask a seven-part question about this.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: But, I mean, could you talk— would you have cut rates by 50 basis points if the market had been pricing in, like, low odds of a 50 point move like they were last Wednesday, you know, after the CPI number came out?

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: It was a really small probability of a 50 point cut.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: Does that play in your consideration at all?

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: Just talk a little bit about that.

speaker: GREG ROBB
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re always going to try to do what we think is the right thing for the economy at that time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we’ll do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we did today.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Simon.

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: Simon Rabinovitch with the Economist.

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: You’ve mentioned how closely you’re watching the labor market, but you also noted that payroll numbers have been a little bit less reliable lately because of the big downward revisions.

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: Does that put your focus overwhelmingly on the unemployment rate?

speaker: SIMON RABINOVITCH
sentence: And given the SEP projection of 4.4 [percent] basically being the peak in the cycle, would going above that be the kind of thing that would trigger another 50 basis point cut?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we will continue to look at that broad array of labor market data, including the payroll numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not discarding those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, we’ll certainly look at those, but we will mentally tend to adjust them based on the QCEW adjustment, which you referred to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There isn’t a bright line.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it will be—the unemployment rate’s very important, of course, but there isn’t a single statistic or single bright line over which that thing that might move that would dictate one thing or another.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll look at—each meeting, we’ll look at all the data on inflation, economic activity, and the labor market, and we’ll make decisions about, is our policy stance where it needs to be to foster over the medium term our mandate goals?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I can’t—I can’t say we have a bright line in mind.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Matt Egan.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Thanks, Chair Powell.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Matt Egan from CNN.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: I know that you discussed earlier how the Fed does whatever the right thing is and nothing else factors in.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: But, in general, can you talk about whether or not you believe a sitting U.S. president should have a say in Fed decisions on interest rates?

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Because that’s something that former President Trump, who obviously appointed you, has previously suggested.

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: And I know the Fed is designed to be independent, but why?

speaker: MATT EGAN
sentence: Can you tell the public why you view that as so important?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So countries that are—democracies around the world, countries that are sort of like the United States, all have what are called independent central banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the reason is that people have found over time that insulating the central bank from direct control by political authorities avoids making monetary policy in a way that favors maybe people who are in office as opposed to people who are not in office.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s the idea, is that—you know, I think the data are clear that countries that have independent central banks, they get lower inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so we’re, we’re not—we do our work to serve all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not serving any politician, any political figure, any cause, any issue, nothing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just maximum employment and price stability on behalf of all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s how the other central banks are set up, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a good institutional arrangement, which has been good for the public and I hope—and I hope and strongly believe that it will continue.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Kyle.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: Kyle Campbell for American Banker.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: Thanks for taking the questions, Chair Powell.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: A couple regulatory developments in the past week that I want to ask you about.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: First, last week Vice Chair for Supervision Michael Barr outlined his views for the changes to the Basel III endgame.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: I’m wondering if you are in alignment with him on what those changes should be, if those have support on the Board in the broad way that you’re looking for, and if you think the other agencies are also fully onboard with that approach.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: And then yesterday, other banking regulators— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: You know what, hold the second question.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: Okay.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll give you the second question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the answer to your question is that, yes, those, those changes were negotiated between the agencies with my support and with my involvement, with the idea that we were going to re-propose, re-propose the changes that Vice Chair Barr talked about and then take comment on them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, yes, that is—that’s happening with my support.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: Is there a date for that— CHAIR POWELL.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: That’s not a final proposal, though, you understand.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: We’re putting them out for comment.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: We’re going to take comment and make appropriate changes.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: We don’t have a—we don’t have a calendar date for that, and, as for the other agencies, you know, the idea is that we’re all moving together, we’re not moving separately, so that—I don’t know exactly where that is.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: But the idea is that we will move as a group to put this, again, out for comment, and then, you know, it’ll—the comments will come back 60 days later, and we’ll dive into them, and we’ll try to bring this to a conclusion sometime in the first half of next year.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: Right.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: And then, yesterday.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: there were merger reform finalizations from the other bank regulators.

speaker: KYLE CAMPBELL
sentence: What does the Fed have to do to align itself on a merger?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, I would—I would bounce that question to Vice Chair Barr.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a good question, but I don’t have that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thanks.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Jennifer, for the last question.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Thank you, Chair Powell.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Jennifer Schonberger with Yahoo Finance.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: You said earlier that the decision today reflects with appropriate recalibration strength in the labor market that could be maintained in the context of moderate growth, even though the policy statement says you view the risks to inflation and job growth as roughly balanced.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Given what you’ve said, though, today, I’m curious, are you more worried about the job market and growth than inflation?

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Are they not roughly balanced?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, I think—I think, and we think, they are now roughly balanced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you go back for a long time, the risks were on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We had a historically tight labor market, historically tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There was a severe labor shortage, so very hot labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we had inflation way above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, that said to us, concentrate on inflation, concentrate on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we did for a while, and we kept at that, that the stance that we put in place 14 months ago was a stance that was focused on bringing down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Part of bringing down inflation, though, is cooling off the economy and a little bit cooling off the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You now have a cooler labor market, in part because of our activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So what that tells you is, it’s time to change our stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we did that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The sense of the change in the stance is that we’re recalibrating our policy over time to a stance that will be more neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And today was—I think we made a good strong start on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it was the right decision, and I think it should send a signal that we, you know, that we’re committed to coming up with a good outcome here.

speaker: JENNIFER SCHONBERGER
sentence: Is the economy more vulnerable to a shock now that could tip it into recession?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t—there’s—as I look—well, let me look at it this way: I don’t see anything in the economy right now that suggests that the likelihood of a recession—sorry, of a downturn is elevated, okay?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see—you see growth at a solid rate, you see inflation coming down, and you see a labor market that’s, that’s still at very solid levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so I don’t really see that, no.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: MICHELLE SMITH
sentence: Thank you.
